accuracy.evidence: Counting language and principles match Development Matters (2021) 3-4 Mathematics: one number for each item (one-to-one), the last number counted gives how many (cardinal principle), and comparing with 'more than' and 'fewer than'. Every scene was checked by hand: plates of 4, 7 and 6; jars of 5, 8 and 6 against Show me guesses 4, 8 and 9 give more than, same as, fewer than; sensible picks 5 for 6, 8 for 9, 3 for 3, 6 for 7; size pairs 4 vs 7 (right), 6 vs 3 (left), 5 vs 5 (same); spread rows 5/5 same, 6/4 top, 3/3 same. All groups stay within 10.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-counting errors named in the adult text: guess must be exact (predict step 2, p5, challenge 'exact'), wild guesses (sensible-guess scene, m3, challenge 'big'), double-counting or skipping (repeat taps flagged in step 1 and 2, m4, challenge 'twice'), reciting the list instead of the cardinal number (m1, challenge 'last'), bigger objects mean more (predict step 4, p4, m7, challenge 'size') and Piagetian non-conservation where a longer row looks like more (predict step 5, m5, challenge 'spread').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagguess is built around estimate-then-check: a guess keypad of 1 to 10 before a jar is counted, numbered tags that appear on each tapped item with double-tap detection, a more/fewer/same comparison against the child's own guess, sensible-versus-giant guess choices, big-versus-small object jars and a slider that spreads a row of cars. It is not a rote-counting, subitising or ten-frame lab; the lab_distinct gate passes under 30% against every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child finds the ideas by doing: each tapped item gets its number and a repeat tap is ringed red with 'it is number 3 already'; after counting a jar the child must compare the count to their own guess and is told how far away it was; a wrong size or spread verdict reveals numbered counts on both sides. The step summaries confirm what was just counted.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'Yes, it was wrong' for a guess of 4 against a count of 5 (the lab calls 1 away a close guess), 'The apples, they look fuller' (counting shows 7 blueberries beat 4 apples), and 'Yes, the row is longer' for spread cars (the count stays 5).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; wrong options are tagged with six specific messages: exact (close is good), size (big things fill space, not number), big (giant numbers are not good guesses), last (the last number tells how many), spread (longer row, same number), twice (counting one twice makes the number too big). Answer order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences with numbers a 3 to 4 year old knows (up to 7) and concrete things (sweets, apples, cars); lab prompts are under 30 words with one instruction each. Adult text names the curriculum terms (cardinal principle, one-to-one correspondence) once and stays inside the validator's adult limit.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs: guess; count to check; compare to the guess; size and spread tricks. Adult paragraphs: curriculum placement, home practice, common mistakes, what the lab does. No stock phrases, and the content gate's filler and duplicate checks pass.

mobile.evidence: Below 520 px the canvas uses a 1.15 ratio; items are spread on a seeded grid sized to the area so tap targets are at least 44 px (hit radius max of 1.25 r and 22 px), the guess keypad shrinks to 10 keys about 30 px wide on canvas but every key has a full-size button twin below. The iPhone 13 walkthrough completes every Show me.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin (Touch the next one, Guess 1 to 10, More than / Fewer than / Same as my guess, the sensible guesses, More apples / More blueberries / The same number, Spread the bottom row and the row verdicts). The canvas aria-label reports every count, slider value and verdict; axe WCAG 2.1 AA runs clean in light and dark themes.
